title: Top 3D Printers for Beginners & Hobbyists (2026)
summary: The Bambu Lab X2D is the best all-round pick, the A1 Mini and Anycubic Kobra X are the best budget starts, and the Prusa Core One is the premium choice.
method: Picks come from Tom's Hardware (updated Oct 6, 2026) and TechRadar (updated Sep 16, 2026), and every model listed is named by both. All3DP's roundup also names the A1 Mini and the Prusa Core One.
assumptions: Prices move a lot, especially Bambu Lab sales, so we quote list or launch prices only where a source states one and tell you who said it. We left out TechRadar's overall pick, the Bambu Lab H2D, because it costs well over $1,500 and this guide targets beginners and hobbyists. Resin printers (for miniatures) are a separate category and are not covered here.

products.name: Bambu Lab X2D
why: Tom's Hardware names the X2D its best 3D printer overall, calling it the successor to the X1C that started the consumer boom. It is a fast CoreXY machine with quick-swap dual nozzles, active chamber heating and AI camera monitoring, and it lets you keep the door closed even when printing PLA or PETG.

TechRadar picks it as its top printer for schools and offices. Its reviewer ran it for 250 hours with zero failures across PLA, PETG, carbon-fiber filaments, TPU and multi-material prints, and praised the three-stage air filtration.
specs: Dual-nozzle CoreXY, enclosed (both sources)
About 256 mm build cube (Tom's Hardware)
$649 standalone, $899 with the AMS 2 Pro multicolor Combo (Tom's Hardware, Oct 2026)
5-inch touchscreen; send models from the Bambu Handy app (Tom's Hardware)
pros: Simple to use, with easy nozzle swaps and auto bed leveling
Handles tougher filaments out of the box
Quiet and well filtered for a desk or classroom
cons: The second nozzle uses a slower Bowden drive limited to about 200 mm/s (TechRadar)
Assigning filaments for dual-nozzle prints still takes some learning
The AMS 2 Pro needs an optional power cord to dry filament while printing (Tom's Hardware)
products.best_for: Buyers who want one printer that will not hold them back as they learn
products.skip_if: You only want the cheapest way to start, or you will print single-color PLA only

products.name: Bambu Lab A1 Mini
why: TechRadar's budget pick is the A1 Mini. It scored five stars in the review, needs no manual calibration or assembly, and its optional AMS Lite handles up to four filaments, a feature that is normally reserved for pricier machines.
Tom's Hardware uses the four-color A1 Mini as its example of a printer that makes colorful toys and games easy on a coffee table. It is now several years old, so it is often discounted.
specs: 180 x 180 x 180 mm build volume (TechRadar)
Open frame, no enclosure
Up to four colors with AMS Lite
About $219 in TechRadar's price roundup; Tom's Hardware listed it at $209 on sale at Best Buy
cons: Filament swaps are slow and the touchscreen is less responsive (TechRadar)
No enclosure, so not ideal for ABS or ASA
products.best_for: First-time buyers on a tight budget and small desks
products.skip_if: You want to print large parts or tougher materials

products.name: Anycubic Kobra X
why: Tom's Hardware names the Kobra X its best budget 3D printer. It is a four-color machine by default thanks to a small multi-material unit built into the tool head. In their head-to-head test, a color swap took about 35 seconds against 90 seconds or more on the Bambu A1, which saved roughly 10 hours on a 776-swap print.
TechRadar picks it as the best printer for beginners, praising the guided setup, the clear calibration steps and the consistent first layers with both PLA and PETG.
specs: 260 x 260 x 260 mm build volume (both sources)
Native four-color printing
Open frame (TechRadar)
Tom's Hardware cites a $279 launch price; check the current price
pros: Larger bed than the A1 Mini
cons: Still produces purge waste, about 27% less than rivals in Tom's Hardware's test
Spool holder makes loading awkward; non-Anycubic filament can be fiddly
products.best_for: Beginners who want multicolor prints without paying for a Bambu
products.skip_if: You want engineering-grade filaments or an enclosure

products.name: Bambu Lab P2S
why: TechRadar says the Bambu Lab P2S was in the running for best overall in its 3D printer guide and calls it a strong contender. It is an enclosed CoreXY printer with a 256 x 256 x 256 mm build volume, a 500 mm/s top print speed, a 5-inch touchscreen and an AI camera that watches for failed prints.

It is the cheaper enclosed Bambu next to the X2D: Tom's Hardware says the X2D costs only a little more than the P2S, and the X2D adds active chamber heating, which the P2S does not have. For multicolor you need the Combo, which adds the AMS 2 Pro.

products.name: Bambu Lab A1
why: TechRadar says the A1 is ideal for most people and general use: small, fun and easy, with good print quality, ultra-fast printing and multi-filament versatility. Tom's Hardware used it as the rival in its head-to-head test of the Anycubic Kobra X, and TechRadar suggests it as an alternative to the Kobra X for beginners.
The trade-offs are the complex software, the lack of an enclosure and an 80°C bed limit (TechRadar), and slower color swaps than the newest tool-head designs (Tom's Hardware).
specs: Open frame, no enclosure (TechRadar)
Slightly smaller bed than the Kobra X's 260 mm cube (Tom's Hardware)
Multi-filament capable (TechRadar)
Bambu runs frequent sales, so check the current price
pros: Bigger bed than the A1 Mini
cons: Software is more complex than rivals

products.best_for: People who want a larger open-frame printer from a proven brand
products.skip_if: You need an enclosure or the quickest color changes

products.name: Prusa Core One
why: Tom's Hardware names the Core One its best premium printer: Prusa's first CoreXY, about 20% faster than the MK4S with slightly better print quality, and an enclosed chamber that can reach 50 degrees Celsius for all filament types. It also comes with a perfect first layer, automatic bed leveling and factory-set input shaping.
TechRadar calls it the best printer for business: professional-grade reliability and repeatable results from PLA to ASA, with PrusaSlicer and Prusa Connect for managing several printers at once.
specs: Fully enclosed CoreXY, up to 50°C chamber (Tom's Hardware)
$1,199 assembled, $949 as a kit (Tom's Hardware); $449 conversion kit for MK4S owners
Auto bed leveling, factory input shaping
pros: Enclosed and very quiet in Tom's Hardware's testing
Upgrade path from the MK4S and plentiful filament profiles in PrusaSlicer
cons: Expensive compared with the Bambu and Elegoo options
products.best_for: Hobbyists and small businesses who value reliability and long-term support
products.skip_if: You are on a budget or just starting out

tips.title: How to choose
items: Tom's Hardware says filament printers are easier to use and safer around kids and pets; resin gives finer detail but means toxic chemicals, a mask, and washing and curing every print.
Treat auto bed leveling as a must.
Tom's Hardware notes you can now find it under $250, so skip printers that make you level by hand.
Match the machine to your filament.
PLA prints on anything, PETG and TPU need hotends that reach about 220 to 230°C, and ABS or nylon need 240 to 250°C and ideally an enclosure (Tom's Hardware).
Tom's Hardware calls 250 mm cubed and above large format for desktop printers, and 150 to 220 mm average.

faq: Do I need an enclosed printer?

Only if you plan to print ABS, ASA or nylon. TechRadar notes that an open frame like the Kobra X limits material choice, while enclosed machines such as the X2D and Core One handle tougher filaments. The Bambu Lab P2S is enclosed too, but it has no active chamber heating.
It is the most fun feature for beginners, but color changes create purge waste. Tom's Hardware measured the Kobra X at about 27% less waste than rivals, still more than a true tool changer.
Which is the cheapest good start?
The Bambu Lab A1 Mini, per TechRadar's budget pick, with the Anycubic Kobra X next if you want a bigger bed and faster color swaps.
